name: /rdb
tagline: Relational database built from Unix shell filters over plain ASCII tables; the 'shell as a 4GL' approach.
description: /rdb from Revolutionary Software of Santa Cruz, California, implemented a relational database as a suite of roughly 130 Unix commands. Tables were variable-length ASCII files, and operators such as sorttable, jointable, row, column and compute read a table on standard input and wrote one on standard output, so queries were ordinary shell pipelines that could mix in grep, awk or any other Unix tool; indexes, a vi-like forms editor, a report writer and menus rounded it out. Rod Manis documented the approach in the 1988 Prentice-Hall book 'UNIX Relational Database Management' and it was ported to Linux, Solaris, AIX, Mac OS X and POSIX Windows. The rdb.com site lapsed around 2021, though the same pipeline-of-table-filters idea survives in Carlo Strozzi's NoSQL and in modern tools such as Miller.
statusNote: Vendor web presence ended around 2021 and the product is no longer sold. For pipeline-style table processing use SQLite, DuckDB or CSV tools.

pricing.notes: Historically sold per license with renewals; no longer available.

scale.notes: Pipelines parallelise across CPU cores naturally, but data is plain text files on one machine.

strengths: Tables are plain text readable by any Unix tool
Relational operators compose with the whole Unix toolbox in pipelines
Pipelines run stages concurrently, using multiple CPUs without extra work
Very small learning curve for shell users
weaknesses: No transactions, concurrency control or crash safety beyond the file system
Text-file storage is slow and bulky for large tables
useCases: Historical reference for shell-based relational tooling
Maintaining very old Unix applications built on /rdb
